There is a particular shade of blue that shows up twice a day and has never been given a proper name, though astronomers have tried. They call it civil twilight — the period after the sun has dropped below the horizon but before true darkness, when the sky still holds enough light to read by, barely, and everything outside takes on the look of a photograph that hasn't fully developed. Painters call it the blue hour, l'heure bleue, and there's something fitting about the fact that even the people most devoted to naming things settled for a description instead of a name. It isn't day. It isn't night. It refuses to commit.

I have a soft spot for things that refuse to commit. Zero, for instance, took humanity an embarrassingly long time to accept, mostly because nobody could decide what kind of thing it was. The Babylonians used a placeholder symbol for "nothing in this column" centuries before anyone thought to treat nothingness as a number you could add or subtract. The Maya arrived at the same idea independently, carving a shell-shape into their calendars to mark absence. It was the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta, around 628 CE, who finally sat down and worked out the rules — what happens when you add zero to a number, what happens when you subtract it, and famously, what happens when you try to divide by it, which he basically declared a problem for someone else to solve later. Zero is not quite a quantity and not quite the absence of one; it's the hinge the rest of arithmetic swings on, and it took a thousand years of false starts before anyone trusted it enough to build on top of it.

The semicolon has a smaller, pettier version of this identity crisis. It was invented in 1494 by the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius, who wanted a mark that could pause a sentence longer than a comma but stop short of the finality of a period — a punctuation mark for thoughts that are related but not quite ready to merge. Ever since, it has been mocked, defended, mocked again. Kurt Vonnegut told writers never to use them, calling them "transvestite hermaphrodites representing absolutely nothing," which is a wonderfully vicious thing to say about a piece of typography. But I think the semicolon gets a bad reputation precisely because of what it's for: it lives in the place where two ideas are close enough to share a sentence but not close enough to dissolve into one, and that in-between space makes people nervous. We like our sentences, like our days, to declare themselves.

Estuaries do the same work that twilight and zero and semicolons do, just with water instead of light or numbers or syntax. Brackish water — the mix that happens where a river gives up and the sea takes over — is technically neither fresh nor salt, and biologically it's one of the most productive environments on the planet, more fertile, acre for acre, than almost any rainforest. The animals that live there have had to evolve a tolerance for ambiguity that animals confined to purely fresh or purely salt water never needed to develop. Salmon do it on purpose, swimming back through the brackish zone as a kind of decompression chamber between two entirely different chemistries of being alive. It's strange that the places we'd be tempted to describe as "neither here nor there" are so often the places where the most is happening.

Language keeps a little zoo of these creatures too — words that contain their own opposite and refuse to pick a side. "Cleave" means to split apart and also to stick together. "Sanction" can mean to permit or to punish. "Dust" can mean to add fine particles to a surface or to remove them. Linguists call these contranyms, or sometimes, more charmingly, Janus words, after the Roman god with two faces who looked forward and backward at once and gave his name to the month that sits between one year and the next. Nobody quite agrees on why languages produce these self-canceling words, though one theory is that opposite meanings often share an underlying action — to cleave with an axe and to cleave to a person both involve a kind of forceful joining of force to surface — and the meaning just drifted to opposite ends of that single gesture over centuries of use.

Even sleep has its smudged border. Hypnagogia is the name for the strange, half-lit stretch between waking and dreaming, when the rational mind has started to loosen its grip but hasn't yet handed the controls over to the unconscious. People in this state report seeing geometric patterns, hearing their name called, having stray thoughts arrive with the force of revelation. Thomas Edison reportedly used to nap holding steel balls over a metal pan — the moment he fell fully asleep, his hand would relax, the balls would clatter down, and he'd wake himself before the dream could fully take hold, capturing whatever fragment of insight had surfaced in that narrow channel. Salvador Dalí did something similar with a spoon. Both men seemed to understand, in their own ways, that the threshold itself was the valuable part — not waking, not sleeping, but the brief unstable country between them.

I notice I keep returning to thresholds, hinges, in-between hours and in-between words, the things that won't resolve into one category or the other. Maybe it's because most of what's interesting about being any kind of mind happens exactly there, in the blue hour rather than at noon or midnight — in the moment before a sentence decides what it's going to mean.
